scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Clean & Prep the House (Most Important First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, dining area, entrance). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and storage spaces. - **Launder bedding, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least dust them). - **Wash windows/mirrors** for a bright, welcoming look. - *Why?* A clean home feels sacred and ready for guests—it’s the foundation for decorations. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decorative Lights)** - **Place diyas** in key areas: - **Entrance** (mandatory for Diwali—use a small table or wall-mounted holder). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Dining area** (if space allows). - **Balcony/porch** (if you have one). - **Use LED string lights** for a modern touch (safe and energy-efficient). - **Marigold garlands** (traditional) or **fairy lights** (for a soft glow). - *Tip:* If short on time, focus on the **entrance and living room** first—they make the biggest impact. ### **3. Quick Decor Updates (Minimal Effort, Big Impact)** - **Hang rangoli** (even a simple design at the entrance or near diyas). - **Place small decorative items**: - **Diwali-themed candles** (scented ones add ambiance). - **Mini statues** (Ganesha, Lakshmi, or lotus motifs). - **Fresh flowers** (marigolds or jasmine for a natural touch). - **Swap out throw pillows/blankets** for festive colors (gold, red, or orange). ### **4. Final Touches (Last-Minute)** - **Set up a small altar** (if you observe puja) with diyas, flowers, and incense. - **Arrange snacks/drinks** in a pretty tray (for guests). - **Test all lights** (diyas, bulbs, etc.) to avoid last-minute issues. - **Spritz air fresheners** (sandalwood or rose-scented) for a fresh feel. ### **5. Day Before Diwali (Quick Checklist)** - **Replenish diyas** (if using oil-based ones). - **Charge phone/laptop** (for photos/videos). - **Set out guest seating** (if hosting). - **Prepare a welcome note** (on the door or entrance). --- ### **Time-Saving Tips:** ✅ **DIY shortcuts**: - Use **glow sticks** (cheap and safe) as temporary diyas. - **Paint rocks** with gold paint for instant decor. - **Buy pre-made rangoli stencils** or use chalk for quick designs. ✅ **Delegate**: - Ask a family member to handle **lighting** while you focus on **cleaning**. - If you have kids, let them help with **hanging garlands or placing small diyas**. ✅ **Skip perfection**: - A few well-placed diyas + a clean entrance look **far more festive** than half-decorated rooms. --- ### **Sample Timeline (If You’re Short on Time):** - **Day 1 (Today)**: Clean + place diyas in entrance/living room. - **Day 2**: Add rangoli, garlands, and small decor items. - **Day 3 (Before Diwali)**: Final touches (lights, snacks, altar). --- **Most important priority?** **Cleanliness + entrance diyas**—they set the tone for guests. If they expect him to help, they should expect the same from you (or adjust expectations). - **Their ultimatum is extreme**, but it’s a **symptom of deeper issues**: - They feel **undervalued** (you’re paying rent but not contributing enough). - They’re **aging and may not have long-term plans** for the house. - They’re **testing boundaries** because the remodel is disrupting their routine. --- ### **Are You the Asshole? (Score: ~0.3/1)** **Not fully, but you’re not entirely blameless either.** - **Why not fully?** - You’re an adult in a **financially dependent** situation (paying rent ≠ freedom from chores). - Their **reaction was disproportionate** (hotel ultimatum is extreme). - **Gaming while they struggle** (flood + remodel) may feel petty, but it’s also **human**—you’re avoiding emotional labor. - **Why some blame?** - **Passive aggression ("in a minute")** is a **coping mechanism**, not a mature response. - **No effort to compromise**—you didn’t even try to help once they asked. - **Brother comparison** is a **common parental tactic**, but it’s still **manipulative** when used to guilt-trip you. - **Their ultimatum is unfair**, but **your refusal to engage** made it harder for them to communicate their needs. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** #### **1. Take Responsibility (But Don’t Apologize for Your Needs)** - **Acknowledge the conflict**: *"I realize I didn’t handle that well. I was distracted, and I should’ve been more respectful."* - **Don’t over-apologize**—this isn’t about guilt, it’s about **restoring trust**. - **Offer a compromise**: *"I’ll help with groceries next time, but I need to set boundaries. Can we discuss how we can work together better?"* #### **2. Address the Root Issue: The Remodel & Your Future** - **Ask them directly**: *"This remodel is a big change. Do you still want me to live here long-term, or is this a sign that things need to shift?"* - **If they’re checking a hotel**, they may be **testing the waters** to see if you’ll leave. **Don’t rush out**—but **don’t stay out of obligation**. - **Propose a trial period**: *"Let’s see how the remodel goes. If it’s too disruptive, I’ll start looking for a place."* #### **3. Rebuild Trust (But Protect Your Space)** - **Small gestures help**: - Help with **one task** (e.g., carrying in a few bags). - **Check in on them** (they’re stressed about the remodel). - **But don’t let it become a chore**. If they expect **constant help**, that’s **exploitation**. #### **4. Prepare for the Next Phase** - **If they want you to leave by Friday**, **don’t panic**—but **start planning**. - Look for **short-term rentals** (Airbnb, extended stays). - **Negotiate**: *"I can help with the move if you give me more time."* - **If they stay**, **set clearer boundaries**: - *"I’ll help with [X tasks], but I need [Y] time for myself."* - **Don’t let them guilt-trip you** with comparisons to your brother. --- ### **Long-Term Perspective** - **This isn’t just about groceries**—it’s about **adulthood, independence, and respect**. - **Staying forever is a choice**, but **passive resistance won’t make them happy**. - **Their ultimatum is extreme**, but **your avoidance has created this mess**. - **The best outcome?** A **mutually respectful agreement** where: - You **contribute** (but not at the cost of your well-being). - They **acknowledge your adulthood** (not just your rent payment). - You **both have clear expectations** about the future. --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Not the Villain… But You’re Not the Hero Either** You’re **not wrong for prioritizing your time**, but **your approach escalated the conflict**. The real issue is **unspoken expectations**—and now, you have to **fix it before it destroys the relationship**. **What’s the worst that could happen?** - They kick you out (unlikely, but possible if they’re that frustrated). - You move out anyway (which may be healthier for both of you). **What’s the best that could happen?** - You **compromise**, **communicate**, and **find a way to coexist**—or transition out **on your terms**. --- ### **TL;DR:** - **Not fully the asshole**, but **your actions contributed to the blowup**. - **Their reaction was extreme**, but **your avoidance made it worse**. - **Now, you have to fix it**—either by **compromising** or **preparing to leave**. - **Adulting isn’t about being perfect—it’s about being honest and fair.** Would you like help drafting a message to them to start the conversation?
